meta.trial_name: HOPE-3 (Heart Outcomes Prevention Evaluation-3), cholesterol-lowering comparison
meta.drug: rosuvastatin 10 mg/day vs placebo (one comparison of a 2x2 factorial trial; the other factor was candesartan 16 mg + hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg vs placebo)
meta.sponsor: Population Health Research Institute (McMaster University / Hamilton Health Sciences); funded by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and AstraZeneca
meta.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) at a fixed moderate dose, without dose titration or lipid targets, to lower LDL-C
meta.indication: primary prevention of major cardiovascular events in intermediate-risk people (about 1% annual risk) without cardiovascular disease and with average lipid levels, ethnically diverse population in 21 countries

n_randomized.quote: In one comparison from a 2-by-2 factorial trial, we randomly assigned 12,705 participants in 21 countries who did not have cardiovascular disease and were at intermediate risk to receive rosuvastatin at a dose of 10 mg per day or placebo.
n_randomized.note: 6361 rosuvastatin, 6344 placebo (Results; Table 1). Registry S3 enrollment 12705 (actual).

median_followup.note: 5.6 years converted to months (5.6 x 12). Design paper S4 expected a mean of 5.8 years; the sample-size calculation assumed a mean of 5.5 years.

primary_endpoint.value: Two coprimary outcomes: (1) composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke; (2) the first plus revascularization, heart failure, and resuscitated cardiac arrest
primary_endpoint.quote: The first coprimary outcome was the composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke, and the second coprimary outcome additionally included revascularization, heart failure, and resuscitated cardiac arrest.
primary_endpoint.note: The secondary outcome (second coprimary plus angina with evidence of ischemia) 'was adopted by the steering committee in July 2015 without a protocol amendment before unblinding of the data on November 3, 2015. At the same time, a prespecified renal outcome was removed because of limitations of statistical power.' The coprimary outcomes were unchanged and match registry S3.

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Men >=55 and women >=65 years with at least one cardiovascular risk factor (elevated waist-to-hip ratio, history of low HDL-C, current or recent smoking, dysglycemia, family history of premature coronary disease, mild renal dysfunction), or women >=60 with at least two; no cardiovascular disease; no indication for or contraindication to statins, ARBs, ACE inhibitors or thiazides; no lipid or blood-pressure entry thresholds; 4-week single-blind active run-in
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: The trial included men 55 years of age or older and women 65 years of age or older who had at least one of the following cardiovascular risk factors: elevated waist-to-hip ratio, history of a low level of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, current or recent tobacco use, dysglycemia, family history of premature coronary disease, and mild renal dysfunction
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Also: 'The trial did not mandate specific lipid or blood-pressure levels for entry.' Intermediate risk was 'defined as an annual risk of major cardiovascular events of approximately 1%'. Run-in: 'Eligible participants entered a single-blind run-in phase, during which they received active treatments (both for blood-pressure lowering and for cholesterol lowering) for 4 weeks.'

planned_events.note: NOT FOUND: the main paper sizes the trial by sample size (12,700) and an expected event rate of 1% per year in the dual-placebo group, not by a target number of events. The Supplementary Appendix and design paper S4 full text were not read. Observed first-coprimary events: 235 + 304 = 539.

assumed_rrr.quote: we estimated that a sample of 12,700 participants would provide the trial with more than 80% power to detect a risk with rosuvastatin that was 22.5% lower than the risk with placebo.
assumed_rrr.note: Assumptions: 'With an expected event rate of 1% per year for the first coprimary outcome in the dual-placebo group (i.e., persons assigned to receive placebo in both the blood-pressure and cholesterol comparisons), a mean follow-up of 5.5 years, cumulative nonadherence rates of 23% in the groups receiving active treatment, and drop-in rates of 11% over a 5-year period'. Quote joined across a two-column PDF layout.

power.quote: would provide the trial with more than 80% power to detect a risk with rosuvastatin that was 22.5% lower than the risk with placebo.

alpha.quote: To preserve the overall type I error rate of 5% for the testing of both coprimary outcomes in both factorial comparisons, the first coprimary outcome was tested at a P value of 0.04 and the second at a P value of 0.02.
alpha.note: Alpha split: first coprimary at 0.04, second coprimary at 0.02; nominal 0.05 for all other analyses. Two-sidedness not stated explicitly in this sentence.

stopped_early.note: Not stopped early: registry S3 overall status COMPLETED, primary completion 2015-12 (actual); S1 reports unblinding on November 3, 2015 and a median follow-up of 5.6 years versus 5.5 years planned. No single sentence states it; inferred.

baseline.quote: the mean LDL cholesterol level was 127.8 mg per deciliter (3.31 mmol per liter)
baseline.location: Results, Lipid and High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein Levels; Table 1
baseline.note: Table 1: 127.8 +/- 36.1 (rosuvastatin) vs 127.9 +/- 36.0 (placebo); central core laboratory. LDL-C missing for 656 and 651 participants.

baseline.quote: the mean apolipoprotein B level was 1.02 g per liter
baseline.location: Results, Lipid and High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein Levels; Table 1
baseline.note: 1.02 g/L converted to 102 mg/dL. Table 1: 1.03 +/- 0.26 vs 1.02 +/- 0.26 g/L.

baseline.quote: At baseline, the mean total cholesterol level was 201.4 mg per deciliter (5.22 mmol per liter)
baseline.location: Results, Lipid and High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein Levels

baseline.note: From Table 1 (HDL 44.7 +/- 13.9 rosuvastatin, 44.9 +/- 13.8 placebo); 44.8 is the average of the two arms, derived.
From Table 1: median 128.8 (IQR 92.9-179.6) rosuvastatin, 126.5 (92.9-176.1) placebo; 127.6 is the average of the two medians, derived.

baseline.quote: The median high-sensitivity C-reactive protein level at baseline was 2.0 mg per liter
baseline.location: Results, Lipid and High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein Levels

baseline.quote: the mean systolic blood pressure was 138.1 mm Hg

baseline.note: NOT FOUND: not reported in the main paper. Total cholesterol 201.4 minus HDL-C ~44.8 = ~157 mg/dL would be a derived estimate only.
NOT FOUND: not reported in the main paper.

biomarker_effects.timepoint: overall mean over the trial (1 year, 3 years, end of trial)
biomarker_effects.method: central core laboratory; lipid subsample (10-20% of participants); method of LDL-C calculation not stated in the main paper
biomarker_effects.quote: overall mean difference, 34.6 mg per deciliter [0.90 mmol per liter] or 26.5%; P<0.001
biomarker_effects.location: Results, Lipid and High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein Levels; Fig. 1; Abstract
biomarker_effects.note: Between-group (rosuvastatin minus placebo) difference; -34.6 mg/dL. Abstract: 'The overall mean low-density lipoprotein cholesterol level was 26.5% lower in the rosuvastatin group than in the placebo group.' Fig. 1 legend: 'Only data from participants for whom lipid levels were available at all four time points were used in the analyses' (about 480-508 per arm).

biomarker_effects.timepoint: 1 year (also 3 years and end of trial)
biomarker_effects.quote: The LDL cholesterol level (measured in the subsample of participants described in the Methods section) was 39.6 mg per deciliter (1.02 mmol per liter) lower in the rosuvastatin group than in the placebo group at 1 year, 34.7 mg per deciliter (0.90 mmol per liter) lower at 3 years, and 29.5 mg per deciliter (0.76 mmol per liter) lower at the end of the trial
biomarker_effects.location: Results, Lipid and High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein Levels
biomarker_effects.note: 1-year difference (the CTT convention). No 1-year percentage is given in the paper; 39.6/127.8 = 31% vs baseline would be derived only. The ACC press release S2 says 'a drop in low-density lipoprotein, or LDL, cholesterol of 39.6 mg/dL, about 25 percent, after 12 months'. Authors: the LDL-C and apoB differences 'were approximately one quarter smaller by the end of the trial than they were at 1 year', attributed to reduced adherence and statin drop-in on placebo.

biomarker_effects.quote: 0.23 g per liter (22.0%) in the apolipoprotein B level
biomarker_effects.note: -0.23 g/L converted to -23 mg/dL. Results text: 'the overall mean apolipoprotein B level was 0.23 g per liter lower in the rosuvastatin group than in the placebo group (P<0.001 for both comparisons)'.

biomarker_effects.quote: The overall mean triglyceride level was 21.2 mg per deciliter (0.24 mmol per liter) lower
biomarker_effects.location: Results, Lipid and High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein Levels

biomarker_effects.quote: the overall C-reactive protein level was significantly lower in the rosuvastatin group than in the placebo group (log-transformed mean difference, 0.19 mg per liter; P<0.001).
biomarker_effects.location: Results, Lipid and High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein Levels
biomarker_effects.note: A log-scale difference, not a percentage; benefit was consistent across CRP subgroups.
NOT FOUND: on-treatment HDL-C and non-HDL-C differences are not reported in the main paper (Supplementary Appendix not read).

biomarker_effects.quote: Rosuvastatin was associated with highly significant dose-dependent reductions in LDL cholesterol compared with placebo (p <0.001); decreases ranged from 34% (1 mg) to 65% (80 mg).
biomarker_effects.note: Phase 2 dose-ranging (n=142 + 64), published 2001, before readout. The 10 mg value is not stated in the abstract, so change_pct is left null; the abstract adds 'an additional 4.5% LDL cholesterol reduction for each doubling of the rosuvastatin dose'. In hypercholesterolemic patients over 6 weeks; much larger than the 26.5% ITT difference in HOPE-3, which was diluted by nonadherence and drop-in over 5.6 years.

hr.unit: hazard ratio (first coprimary outcome, rosuvastatin vs placebo)
hr.quote: The first coprimary outcome occurred in 235 participants (3.7%) in the rosuvastatin group and in 304 participants (4.8%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.64 to 0.91; P = 0.002).
hr.note: Second coprimary: 277 (4.4%) vs 363 (5.7%), HR 0.75 (0.64-0.88), P<0.001. Secondary outcome HR 0.77 (0.66-0.89). Table 2 components: CV death 154 vs 171, HR 0.89 (0.72-1.11); MI 45 vs 69, HR 0.65 (0.44-0.94); stroke 70 vs 99, HR 0.70 (0.52-0.95); revascularization 0.68 (0.48-0.95); death from any cause 334 vs 357, HR 0.93 (0.80-1.08), P=0.32. NNT 91 (first coprimary) and 73 (second). Extended follow-up S14 (8.7 years): 21% reduction in MACE-1 (95% CI 0.69-0.90).

p.quote: hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.64 to 0.91; P = 0.002
p.note: Below the allocated threshold of 0.04 for the first coprimary outcome.

events_treatment.quote: The first coprimary outcome occurred in 235 participants (3.7%) in the rosuvastatin group

events_control.quote: in 304 participants (4.8%) in the placebo group
events_control.note: Placebo arm N=6344. Total first-coprimary events 539. Observed placebo rate 4.8% over 5.6 years (~0.86%/year, derived) vs the assumed 1%/year in the dual-placebo group.

safety_signals.value: Muscle pain or weakness: 367 (5.8%) vs 296 (4.7%), P=0.005; discontinuation for muscle symptoms 1.3% vs 1.2% (P=0.63); rhabdomyolysis or myopathy 2 vs 1
safety_signals.quote: More participants in the rosuvastatin group than in the placebo group had muscle pain or weakness (367 [5.8%] vs. 296 [4.7%], P = 0.005).
safety_signals.note: Discussion: 'these conditions were generally reversible with temporary discontinuation. There was only one case of rhabdomyolysis (in the rosuvastatin group)'.

safety_signals.quote: placebo group underwent cataract surgery (241 [3.8%] vs. 194 [3.1%], P = 0.02).
safety_signals.note: Authors: 'This effect has not been reported in trials but has been seen in observational studies.' and 'Determining whether the excess in cataracts is related to the treatment requires a systematic analysis of all statin trials.'

safety_signals.value: No excess of new-onset diabetes: 232 (3.9%) vs 226 (3.8%), HR 1.02 (0.85-1.23), P=0.82
safety_signals.quote: There was no significant difference between the two groups in the number of participants who had new-onset diabetes (Table 2).
safety_signals.note: Contrasts with JUPITER (rosuvastatin 20 mg), which reported 'a higher incidence of physician-reported diabetes' (S11), and with the on-target HMGCR diabetes effect in genetics (S9).

safety_signals.value: No excess cancer (267 vs 286) or liver abnormalities; fewer discontinuations of rosuvastatin than placebo (23.7% vs 26.2%)
safety_signals.quote: Rosuvastatin was permanently discontinued in fewer participants than was placebo (1510 [23.7%] vs. 1664 [26.2%], P = 0.001).
safety_signals.location: Results, Participants and Adherence; Results, Safety
safety_signals.note: Cancer 267 and 286 (Results, Safety). Discussion: 'there was no excess in diabetes or functional abnormalities of the liver in the rosuvastatin group.'

safety_signals.value: Slightly more hemorrhagic strokes (11 vs 8) with fewer ischemic strokes (41 vs 77)
safety_signals.quote: Fewer ischemic strokes occurred in the rosuvastatin group than in the placebo group (41 vs. 77), but slightly more hemorrhagic strokes occurred (11 vs. 8)
safety_signals.note: Small numbers; no test reported. Also fewer venous thromboembolic events (14 vs 31; HR 0.45, 0.24-0.84).

safety_signals.value: No significant reduction in cardiovascular or all-cause death: CV death HR 0.89 (0.72-1.11); all-cause death 334 vs 357, HR 0.93 (0.80-1.08), P=0.32
safety_signals.quote: The total number of deaths was 334 in the rosuvastatin group and 357 in the placebo group
safety_signals.note: Not a harm signal; a limit of the benefit in a low-event-rate population.

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization: HMGCR (statin target) LDL-lowering variants protect against cardiovascular events, with the same effect per unit LDL-C as PCSK9 variants
genetics.effect: OR 0.81 (0.72-0.90) per 10 mg/dL lower LDL-C for the HMGCR score
genetics.quote: Variants in PCSK9 and HMGCR were associated with nearly identical protective effects on the risk of cardiovascular events per decrease of 10 mg per deciliter (0.26 mmol per liter) in the LDL cholesterol level: odds ratio for cardiovascular events, 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74 to 0.89) for PCSK9 and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.72 to 0.90) for HMGCR.

genetics.finding: HMGCR variants lower LDL-C and slightly raise type 2 diabetes risk and body weight, mirroring the statin diabetes signal (an on-target effect); available before the HOPE-3 readout
genetics.effect: 0.06 mmol/L lower LDL-C per rs17238484-G allele; T2D OR 1.02 (1.00-1.05) per allele; statin vs placebo trials T2D OR 1.11 (1.03-1.20)
genetics.quote: The increased risk of type 2 diabetes noted with statins is at least partially explained by HMGCR inhibition.

genetics.finding: LDL-C is causal; CTT meta-analysis of statin trials: about 22% fewer major vascular events per 1.0 mmol/L LDL-C reduction, with no threshold
genetics.quote: similar proportional reductions in major vascular events per 1·0 mmol/L LDL cholesterol reduction were found in all types of patient studied (rate ratio [RR] 0·78, 95% CI 0·76-0·80; p<0·0001), including those with LDL cholesterol lower than 2 mmol/L on the less intensive or control regimen.

genetics.finding: CTT low-risk meta-analysis: the proportional benefit per mmol/L LDL-C is at least as large in people at low baseline risk (5-year risk <10%) as in higher-risk people
genetics.effect: RR 0.79 (0.77-0.81) per 1.0 mmol/L overall; 0.62 and 0.69 in the two lowest risk categories
genetics.quote: The proportional reduction in major vascular events was at least as big in the two lowest risk categories as in the higher risk categories

consensus_explanation.summary: In HOPE-3, rosuvastatin 10 mg in 12,705 intermediate-risk, mostly non-white people without cardiovascular disease and with average LDL-C (mean 127.8 mg/dL) lowered LDL-C by 26.5% on average (0.90 mmol/L; 1.02 mmol/L at 1 year). It cut the first coprimary outcome by 24% (235 vs 304 events; HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64-0.91, P=0.002, well below the allocated 0.04), with consistent effects on the second coprimary outcome (HR 0.75, 0.64-0.88), MI and stroke, and across subgroups of baseline risk, LDL-C, CRP, blood pressure and ethnicity. The investigators judged the size of the benefit consistent with the LDL-C reduction seen in earlier statin trials, which fits the CTT per-mmol/L relationship (RR 0.78 per mmol/L, about 0.80 expected for 0.90 mmol/L, derived) and HMGCR genetics; reviews (USPSTF evidence review, Am J Med review) counted it as solid evidence for statins in lower-risk primary prevention, and the benefit persisted in 8.7-year follow-up. The caveats are modest: an excess of muscle symptoms (5.8% vs 4.7%) and cataract surgery (3.8% vs 3.1%), no significant reduction in cardiovascular or all-cause death, a small absolute benefit at about 0.9% annual risk (NNT 91), and, per one review, no significant reduction among women when analyzed alone. The NEJM editorial (Cushman and Goff) was not read.

open_questions: Which LDL-C contrast to feed the calculator: the overall mean difference (-0.90 mmol/L, -26.5%; the paper's headline) or the 1-year difference (-1.02 mmol/L; the CTT convention). The calc file uses the overall mean. Derived CTT check: 0.78^0.90 = 0.80 and 0.78^1.02 = 0.78, vs observed HR 0.76 (0.64-0.91); both fit within the CI.
Lipids were measured only in a 10-20% subsample, and the Fig. 1 analysis used only participants with all four measurements (~480-508 per arm).
Planned number of events not stated in the main paper; sizing was by sample size and an assumed 1%/year dual-placebo event rate. The observed placebo rate (4.8% over 5.6 years) was a little lower.

The ACC press release says the 12-month LDL-C drop of 39.6 mg/dL was 'about 25 percent'; the paper gives 26.5% as the overall mean difference and no 1-year percentage (39.6/127.8 = 31% vs baseline, derived).
The Cushman and Goff NEJM editorial (S5) was not read (paywalled); the expert view relies on S1, S12, S13, S14, S16 and the CTT and genetics papers.
On-treatment HDL-C, non-HDL-C and Lp(a) differences were not reported in the main paper; the Supplementary Appendix was not read.
Cataract-surgery excess (P=0.02) was flagged by the authors as needing confirmation across statin trials; no follow-up source was read.
Women: one review (S13) notes no significant reduction in women alone; the main paper reports no heterogeneity by sex.
